title: What makes up Shareholders' Equity?
subtitle: The components of equity - from paid-in capital to retained earnings
openingQuestion: What does negative Retained Earnings (an accumulated deficit) mean?
openingOptions: The company has paid out far too much in dividends over recent years
The company's cumulative losses exceed its total historical profit
The company is losing money this year
explanation: Shareholders' equity has a part contributed by shareholders - paid-in capital plus issuance premium - and a part made of profit the company has kept over the years, minus treasury shares bought back. Negative retained earnings means historical losses exceed historical profit, which is quite normal for a business in a cash-burning growth phase. Conversely, a business that has bought back stock for years can carry very thin equity while remaining perfectly healthy.

realWorldExample.description: MWG's balance sheet shows equity consisting of shareholder-contributed capital (the par value of shares issued), share premium (the gap between issue price and par value), undistributed after-tax profit (retained earnings) accumulated over many years, and treasury stock whenever MWG buys back shares for ESOP grants or buybacks.

quiz.question: How does Treasury Stock affect equity?
options: It increases the total liabilities on the balance sheet
It increases equity, because the company owns more shares
No effect, since it's just an internal transaction
It decreases equity, as a deduction adjustment
quiz.explanation: When a company buys back its own shares, that stock becomes treasury stock and is subtracted from equity. This is why a large buyback can even push equity negative.

quiz.question: Why might a company with large positive Retained Earnings still need to raise capital by issuing new shares?
options: Only a loss-making company would ever need to issue new shares
Because retained earnings is an accounting figure, not cash
This can't happen, since positive retained earnings always comes with matching cash
Because retained earnings is always exactly equal to the current cash balance
quiz.explanation: This is a common confusion: Retained Earnings reflects CUMULATIVE UNDISTRIBUTED PROFIT, not AVAILABLE CASH. Prior years' profit may already have been reinvested into plant, inventory, or receivables - no longer sitting as cash ready to use.

quiz.question: What does Additional Paid-in Capital (APIC) reflect?
options: The cumulative profit the company has retained
The gap between the issue price and the par value of the shares
The value of treasury shares bought back from the market
The total long-term bank borrowing the company currently has
quiz.explanation: APIC records the real amount a company raises above its nominal par value - for example, a par value of 10,000 dong but an IPO price of 50,000 dong puts the 40,000 dong difference per share into APIC.

quiz.question: A company just IPO'd, raising 1,000 billion dong. Where does this money mainly show up in Shareholders' Equity?
options: Retained Earnings, since it's new cash flowing in
Treasury Stock, since shares were just issued
Common Stock and APIC, since this is new contributed capital
Not in Equity at all, only in the cash flow statement
quiz.explanation: IPO proceeds are capital contributed by new shareholders, not profit the company earned itself - so it adds into Common Stock (par value) and mostly into APIC (the issue-price premium), not Retained Earnings.

quiz.question: Company A pays a cash dividend of 200 billion dong. How does this affect Shareholders' Equity?
options: No effect, since the dividend is paid out of available cash
It increases Retained Earnings because shareholders receive money
It increases Treasury Stock by an equivalent amount of cash
It decreases Retained Earnings, lowering total Equity
quiz.explanation: Paying a dividend redistributes part of accumulated profit to shareholders - Retained Earnings falls by exactly the dividend paid, pulling total Equity down along with it, while Cash also falls on the asset side.

quiz.question: Two companies in the same industry have equal total Equity, but Company X's equity is 80% Retained Earnings while Company Y's is 80% APIC. What does this difference tell you?
options: X built its equity from profit, Y relies on outside contributed capital
No real difference, since equal total Equity is all that matters
Company X must have been losing money for several years in a row
Company Y must be carrying more debt than Company X
quiz.explanation: The same Equity number can hide two very different stories: X created value through its own operations (a good sign of self-sustaining profitability), while Y depends on outside capital - possibly because its model needs heavy funding or hasn't reached stable profitability yet.

quiz.question: When a company issues new shares (a secondary offering) to raise capital, what happens to existing shareholders who don't buy more?
options: The number of shares they hold stays exactly the same
Their ownership percentage gets diluted
They receive proportional free shares in compensation
The Equity value of their stake automatically doubles
quiz.explanation: Issuing more shares raises the total shares outstanding - if existing shareholders don't buy more to keep their proportion, their ownership percentage (and usually EPS) gets diluted, even though the company's absolute Equity may rise thanks to the new capital.

quiz.question: Why is Treasury Stock recorded as a NEGATIVE item within Equity, instead of simply cancelling (removing) the repurchased shares?
options: Because accounting law requires every repurchase to be recorded as negative
Because treasury stock always carries a negative market value
Because the company can reissue it or use it for ESOP grants
Because it is really a liability owed back to the shareholders
quiz.explanation: Treasury stock isn't cancelled right away - the company can reuse it (as ESOP grants for employees, or resell it when it needs capital) - so accounting records it as a deduction from Equity, correctly reflecting the cash spent to reacquire ownership rather than writing it off entirely.

quiz.question: A newly founded tech company has Common Stock of 1 billion, APIC of 500 billion (from a funding round), and Retained Earnings of -300 billion (from accumulated losses). What is total Equity, and is this worrying?
options: Total Equity must always be positive for every startup
Total Equity of 300 billion, close to bankruptcy
Total Equity can't be calculated because one item is negative
Total Equity is 201 billion, and how worried you should be depends on the burn rate
quiz.explanation: 1 + 500 - 300 = 201 billion, Equity is still positive. For a tech startup, negative Retained Earnings (burning cash to grow) is normal - what matters is how much cash runway is left relative to the monthly burn rate, not the negative number itself.

keyTakeaways: Equity consists of: common stock, APIC, retained earnings, treasury stock
Negative retained earnings = an accumulated deficit
Buybacks reduce equity - companies with large buybacks can even show negative equity

practicePrompt.question: A tech company keeps buying back its own shares (a buyback) year after year, making the 'treasury stock' item increasingly negative. Retained earnings stays positive but smaller than the cumulative buyback amount. What could happen to the company's total Equity?
options: Equity is bound to always stay positive and grow, since the company keeps accumulating profit every year
Equity can go negative if treasury stock grows larger than common stock + APIC + retained earnings combined
Equity is never affected by a company buying back its own shares
A buyback only affects Cash Flow and has absolutely no impact on the Equity section of the balance sheet
practicePrompt.explanation: Equity consists of: common stock, APIC, retained earnings, treasury stock. A buyback makes treasury stock more negative, and if a company buys back aggressively for years, total Equity can genuinely turn negative even while the company remains profitable - this isn't necessarily a bad sign, it reflects a policy of returning capital to shareholders.

summary.keyIdea: Equity consists of: common stock, APIC, retained earnings, treasury stock
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Negative retained earnings = an accumulated deficit

application.title: Find a company with an accumulated deficit
application.message: Look up the financial statements of a startup or growth company you know, find the Retained Earnings line - if it's negative, that's an accumulated deficit; note down why you think that is.
application.secondary: Negative retained earnings isn't always a bad sign - it depends on the company's stage.

sections.text: You've learned that the Balance Sheet consists of Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' Equity. But 'Shareholders' Equity' isn't a single number - it's the sum of several pieces, each telling a different story about the origin of the value shareholders hold.
The four main components of Equity

Common Stock is the nominal value of shares issued, usually a small figure with little real economic meaning. Additional Paid-in Capital (APIC) is the gap between what shareholders actually paid for newly issued shares and their par value - this is where the real money a company raised in an IPO or a follow-on offering shows up.

Retained Earnings is the cumulative total of all profit the company has generated since founding, minus dividends paid out. This is usually the largest component at long-established, consistently profitable companies like Vinamilk or FPT. Treasury Stock is a negative item - when a company uses cash to buy back its own shares on the market, those shares aren't cancelled but held in treasury, and the repurchase value is deducted directly from equity.
Why can Retained Earnings go negative?

A young company investing heavily to win market share (as many early-stage tech and e-commerce companies do) can lose money for several years running. When cumulative losses exceed cumulative historical profit, Retained Earnings turns negative - called an accumulated deficit. This doesn't automatically mean the company is about to go bankrupt, but it shows the company has never created positive net value for shareholders since founding, and an investor needs to judge whether the path to profitability is clear.

items: Common Stock - the par value of shares issued, with little economic meaning.
APIC - the real money raised above par value when issuing shares.
Retained Earnings - cumulative profit minus dividends paid, reflecting long-term value creation.
Treasury Stock - a negative item when a company buys back its own shares.

sections.label: Aggressive buybacks can push Equity negative
sections.text: Some mature companies with strong cash flow but continuous large-scale buybacks (many US corporations, for example) can carry negative equity on the books - even while remaining extremely healthy in terms of cash flow. This is why you shouldn't look at a single Equity number without looking at its underlying structure.

concepts.def: The par value of common shares issued.
The gap between the actual issue price and the par value of the shares.
Cumulative profit since founding, after dividends paid.
Shares the company bought back from the market, recorded as a negative item within Equity.

lines: Shareholders' equity isn't a simple number - it's the sum of contributed capital, cumulative profit, and adjustments like treasury stock.
Understanding the structure of Equity helps you read the real story: whether a company is building value, burning cash, or returning capital to shareholders.
